text: This paper explores the transmission probabilities in quantum key distribution (QKD) systems over free-space optical (FSO) links. The study investigates the impact of various factors such as atmospheric turbulence, detector efficiency, and channel losses on the transmission probabilities of the QKD system. The authors use a theoretical analysis and numerical simulations to determine the optimal conditions for achieving high transmission probabilities in the presence of these factors. The results of the study can be used to improve the design and performance of QKD systems over FSO links, which have potential applications in secure communication and cryptography.

This study presents a novel approach to the vehicle routing problem by focusing on greenhouse gas emissions and fuel consumption aiming to mitigate adverse environmental effects of transportation. A time-dependent model with time windows is developed to incorporate speed and schedule in transportation. The model considers speed limits for different times of the day in a realistic delivery context. Due to the complexity of solving the model, a simulated annealing algorithm is proposed to find solutions with high quality in a timely manner. Our method can be used in practice to lower fuel consumption and greenhouse gas emissions while total route cost is also controlled to some extent. The capability of method is depicted by numerical examples productively solved within 3.5% to the exact optimal for small and mid-sized problems.

This paper explores the necessary conditions for implementing a regulator that takes into account both momentum and frequency in nonperturbative renormalization group flow equations of out-of-equilibrium statistical systems. The researchers use model A as a benchmark and calculate its dynamical critical exponent, z. They then demonstrate that it is possible to create frequency regulators that conform to causality and the fluctuation-dissipation theorem. The authors also show that the Principle of Minimal Sensitivity (PMS) is an effective method for optimizing critical exponents, but to make the PMS a self-consistent criterion, frequency regulators are needed.

This paper examines the intersection of complexity theory, game theory, and economics, as presented in the Barbados Lectures. The paper provides an overview of the key concepts and theories in each of these fields, and argues that the interdisciplinary approach of the Barbados Lectures offers new and insightful perspectives on the workings of complex economic systems. By incorporating elements of complexity theory, such as non-linear dynamics and self-organizing systems, the paper demonstrates how the traditional models of economic behavior can be enriched and extended. Additionally, the application of game theory provides a deeper understanding of the strategic interactions between economic agents, and the role of information, incentives, and coordination in shaping economic outcomes.

Our solutions describe two parallel, separated bundles of N D1-branes expanding out to form a single orthogonal D3-brane. This configuration corresponds to two charge N magnetic monopoles in the world-volume of a single D3-brane, deforming the D3-brane into two parallel spikes. We obtain the emergent surface corresponding to our nonabelian D1-brane configuration and demonstrate, at finite N, a surprisingly accurate agreement with the shape of the D3-brane world-volume as obtained from the abelian Born-Infeld action. Our solution provides an explicit realization of topology change in noncommutative geometry at finite N.

This paper proposes a novel algorithm for solving the problem of minimizing finite sums with infinite data using a lightweight stochastic optimization approach. The proposed algorithm combines stochastic gradient descent with an adaptive step size selection method to effectively handle the infinite data problem. The algorithm is designed to be computationally efficient by only requiring a subset of the data to be processed at each iteration, while still achieving a high level of accuracy. Theoretical analysis is provided to prove the convergence and optimal convergence rate of the algorithm, and numerical experiments are conducted to demonstrate its effectiveness on a variety of large-scale datasets.

In this chapter, we provide an overview of deception games in three different environments and extend the baseline signaling game models to include evidence through side-channel knowledge acquisition to capture the information asymmetry, dynamics, and strategic behaviors of deception. The MACHO project is one of several teams searching for the dark matter around our Galaxy in the form of Massive Compact Halo Objects (MACHOs). If a compact object passes very close to the line of sight to a background star, the gravitational deflection of light causes an apparent brightening of the star, i.e. a gravitational  microlensing' event. These events will be very rare, so millions of stars must be monitored for many years. We describe our search for microlensing using a very large CCD camera on the dedicated 1.27m telescope at Mt.

Fast and accurate separation of multiple sources from their mixtures is a critical problem in signal processing, with applications ranging from speech enhancement to audio source separation. In this paper, we propose a novel method for multichannel source separation based on the joint diagonalization of spatial covariance matrices. The proposed method exploits the fact that the covariance matrices of the sources are jointly diagonalizable, which can be leveraged to efficiently estimate the mixing matrix and the sources. This paper investigates the development of cooperativeness and competitiveness in children. The study aims to explore how these two traits are shaped by social and cultural factors and how they interact with each other. The research is based on a sample of 200 children aged between 7 to 12 years old from diverse socio-economic and cultural backgrounds. The data collection was conducted using standardized questionnaires and observational methods. The findings suggest that cooperativeness and competitiveness are influenced by a range of factors, including parenting styles, peer relationships, and cultural norms. Additionally, the study found that these traits are not mutually exclusive, as children can display both traits in different contexts.

In this study, we extend the entropy cone to include time-dependent systems, which are relevant for a wide range of physical phenomena, including black holes and quantum systems. This paper argues that the shift towards a public health approach to domestic violence raises significant concerns for individual autonomy and privacy. Medicalized models for addressing domestic violence may not be the most effective means of responding to the problem, and may set problematic precedents for future interventions into intimate relationships. The medicalization of social issues can also result in an over-reliance on diagnostic categories that may not be appropriate for the complexities of domestic violence. Furthermore, by conceptualizing domestic violence through a public health framework, we risk creating a new form of carceral control, where individuals deemed at risk of violence are subjected to surveillance and intervention that may not be warranted.

Once optimal AL behaviour is defined mathematically, reasoning about this abstraction provides insights into AL. In a theoretical context, the optimal selection is compared to existing AL methods, showing that heuristics can make sub-optimal selections. Algorithms are constructed to estimate example quality directly. A large-scale experimental study shows these algorithms to be competitive with standard AL methods.

Is station accessibility split up along racial lines? If so, what remedies might exist under Title VI and/or the ADA to fix that?This Note employs an empirical analysis in order to answer the first question, relying on geospatial data paired with corresponding Census demographic data. The results of the linear and logistic regressions indicate that race is indeed correlated with accessibility levels. In Philadelphia, stations are less likely to be accessible when located in areas with higher concentrations of Black residents, and in New York City, they are less likely to be accessible when located in areas with higher concentrations of Black and, in particular, Black Latinx residents. The Federal Transit Administration ’s forthcoming revised circular offers an opportunity to correct this problem.

Medical experimentation of human subjects is often seen as either ethical or non-ethical, but could there be more nuanced distinctions? This essay explores questions around informed consent, such as whether it means different things depending on various factors, and whether a signature is enough to establish it. The importance of what human subjects are entitled to know before and during clinical trials is highlighted, especially in light of recent controversies surrounding fetal tissue research. The essay offers three contributions: a historical analysis of medical experiments conducted without informed consent, an exploration of how race or status can influence unethical decision-making, and a discussion of how law and ethics can bring about change.

We use a large-scale dataset of thousands of field experiments conducted on Upworthy.com, an online media platform, to investigate the cognitive, motivation, affective, and grammatical factors implementable in messages to motivate people to engage with online content. We map from textual cues measured with Natural Language Processing tools to constructs implied to be relevant by a broad range of prior research literatures. We validate the constructs with human judgment and then test which constructs causally impact click-through to articles when implemented in headlines. Our findings suggest that the use of textual cues identified in previous research and industry advice does impact the effectiveness of headlines overall, but the prior research and industry advice does not always provide useful guidance as to the direction of the effects

Visualizing and navigating through large astronomy images from a remote location with current astronomy display tools can be a frustrating experience in terms of speed and ergonomics, especially on mobile devices. In this paper, we present a high performance, versatile and robust client-server system for remote visualization and analysis of extremely large scientific images. Applications of this work include survey image quality control, interactive data query and exploration, citizen science, as well as public outreach. The proposed software is entirely open source and is designed to be generic and applicable to a variety of datasets. It provides access to floating point data at terabyte scales, with the ability to precisely adjust image settings in real-time. To truly decolonise the curriculum and create a more inclusive teaching and learning environment in HEIs, it is necessary to critically examine the ways in which knowledge is produced and transmitted in the classroom. This requires a deep and sustained commitment to decolonising our pedagogical approach, moving beyond simply adding diverse voices to our reading lists and course materials. One way to approach this is through the use of decolonial pedagogies, which centre the perspectives and experiences of historically marginalised groups and challenge dominant Western epistemologies. These pedagogies involve a rethinking of traditional power structures in the classroom, with an emphasis on co-creating knowledge with students and privileging diverse perspectives and ways of knowing.

This paper explores John Austin's analytical jurisprudence, specifically his version of legal positivism known as empirical-rationalist legal positivism. Through an examination of Austin's key concepts, such as the separation of law and morality, the command theory of law, and the importance of legal language, the paper argues that Austin's approach aimed to establish law as a scientific discipline capable of objective analysis. The paper also explores criticisms of Austin's work, including his failure to account for the complexity of legal systems and the limitations of his emphasis on the sovereign's authority.

Air pollution, particularly CO2 and PM2.5 emissions, poses a significant challenge for many countries globally. Choosing an eco-friendly mode of transportation is an effective strategy for individuals to minimize air pollution in their daily lives. This paper presents a novel approach to measure the impact of eco-friendly transport mode selection on reducing air pollution, using map search logs. Using combinatorial optimization, we formulate the transport mode selection problem, imposing constraints on total CO2 emissions as an example of air pollution, as well as average travel time. Our optimization results demonstrate that the total CO2 emissions can be decreased by 9.23%, while average travel time can also be decreased by 9.96%. The Restricted Isometry Property (RIP) is an important characteristic of matrices when it comes to recovering sparse data. Essentially, a matrix of size m x n satisfies RIP of order k in the l_p norm if the p-norm of the product of the matrix and a vector x is approximately equal to the norm of x, given that x has at most k non-zero entries. Researchers have already investigated the minimum number of rows needed for a matrix to satisfy the RIP, and have established tight bounds. However, in some models used in signal processing, the support of x must belong to a particular family of supports.

Most recently, it has begun to be interpreted as a question about the nature of law, answerable via conceptual analysis. I will argue here that that approach is a mistake. This paper focuses on the impact of link failures and channel noise on distributed consensus algorithms in sensor networks. The paper provides an in-depth analysis of how these factors affect the performance of consensus algorithms and how they can be mitigated. The research is based on simulations and experiments conducted in real-world sensor networks, and the results show that link failures and channel noise can significantly impact the convergence time and accuracy of consensus algorithms. The paper also presents several solutions to overcome these challenges, including the use of redundancy, error correction, and network coding. The results of the study provide insights into the design and implementation of robust consensus algorithms in sensor networks, and have important implications for a wide range of applications, including smart grid management, environmental monitoring, and industrial control systems

This research explores using penalized maximum log-likelihood estimation for exponential family distributions that have a natural parameter within a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. Our approach relies on a new method called doubly dual embedding, which eliminates the need to compute the partition function. This method also enables the creation of a flexible sampling strategy that reduces the cost of Monte-Carlo sampling during the inference stage. The resulting estimator can be extended to kernel conditional exponential families. We establish a link between kernel exponential family estimation and MMD-GANs, which offers a fresh perspective for understanding GANs.

There is ample evidence that perceptions of remorse play a powerful role in criminal cases. However, the most basic question about the evaluation of remorse has received little attention: is remorse something that can be accurately evaluated in a courtroom? We find that the presence of a sharp transition in the dark sector affects significantly the evolution of cosmological perturbations, leading to characteristic features in both spectra. Online social media have significantly altered the manner in which individuals interact with each other and disseminate information, with microblogs becoming particularly important for key activities such as public relations, marketing, and politics. To better comprehend how memes spread within these channels, we have developed an adaptable framework that analyzes, maps, models, and classifies vast microblogging datasets in real-time. This framework powers a web service capable of monitoring political memes on Twitter and identifying instances of astroturfing, smear campaigns, and false information during US elections. Our analysis revealed several instances of abusive behavior online.

Generating a coherent paragraph requires understanding the different relationships between sentences, such as tense and coreference. These relationships are called "flow." To create better flow, we looked at two ways to connect sentences within a paragraph: one is a structure created by humans (e.g., a discourse tree), and the other is a relation learned from the sentences themselves. We created two models that include each form of relation in document-level language models: one is supervised and predicts discourse relations, while the other is unsupervised and uses a recurrent neural network. Our models perform better than baselines in generating partially conditioned paragraphs. The codes and data are available to the public.

This paper presents a novel approach to designing efficient low-redundancy codes for correcting multiple deletions in a sequence. The proposed method is based on the concept of sparse matrices, where the deletion errors are modeled as a sparse vector. Using this model, a codebook is designed that can efficiently correct multiple deletions with low redundancy. The proposed codebook is compared with existing state-of-the-art methods, and simulation results show that it outperforms these methods in terms of correction efficiency, redundancy, and complexity.
